plain_title: When a substance or medicine causes the symptoms
one_liner: Depression, anxiety, psychosis, mania, sleep, or sexual problems caused directly by a substance or a medicine.
in_simple_words: Sometimes mental health symptoms are caused by a substance, during intoxication or withdrawal, or by a prescribed medicine. Heavy drinking can cause depression; stimulants or cannabis can cause psychosis; steroids can cause mania; some medicines cause anxiety or sleep problems. The DSM has a 'substance/medication-induced' version of most disorders. The key sign is timing: symptoms start with use and usually fade within a month of stopping. Treatment focuses on stopping or changing the substance, with support for the symptoms meanwhile.
what_it_can_feel_like: The paranoia started after a weekend of heavy use and faded in two weeks. The doctor called it substance-induced. That mattered for what came next.
I was told I had depression. It was the drinking. Three months sober and it lifted.
A steroid prescription turned my husband into someone I didn't know for a month.
common_signs: Symptoms that start during or soon after using a substance or starting a medicine
Symptoms that are more than the usual effects of the substance
Symptoms fading within about a month of stopping
No history of the same symptoms before the substance
Any disorder: depression, anxiety, psychosis, mania, sleep, sexual, or thinking problems

myths_vs_facts.myth: If a drug caused the psychosis, it isn't real psychosis.
myths_vs_facts.fact: The symptoms are just as real and need care. 'Induced' tells you about the cause, not the seriousness.

myths_vs_facts.myth: Substance-induced means it will always go away on its own.
myths_vs_facts.fact: Most cases improve with abstinence, but some, especially psychosis after heavy stimulant or cannabis use, continue and become a primary disorder. Follow-up matters.

myths_vs_facts.myth: Prescribed medicines can't cause mental health symptoms.
myths_vs_facts.fact: Several can, including steroids, some heart and asthma medicines, and others. Tell your doctor about new symptoms after starting a medicine.

how_common.plain: Substance-induced disorders are common in emergency and addiction settings. Exact rates depend on the substance and the symptom.
how_common.figure: No single figure; the DSM-5-TR gives rates by substance and disorder

what_helps.plain_summary: The main treatment is stopping, reducing, or changing the substance or medicine, safely and with medical advice. Symptoms are supported meanwhile: a safe setting and sometimes short-term medication for psychosis or severe agitation, prescribed and monitored by a doctor. If symptoms don't fade within a month of stopping, the diagnosis is reviewed and treated as a primary disorder. Treatment for the substance use disorder, if there is one, prevents it happening again.
evidence_based_options: Stopping or changing the substance or medicine, with medical guidance
Short-term symptom treatment where needed, prescribed and monitored by a doctor
Reassessment if symptoms persist beyond a month
Treatment for any underlying substance use disorder
self_help_that_supports_care: Telling clinicians honestly what you've taken, including prescribed and over-the-counter medicines
Not stopping a prescribed medicine suddenly without advice
Follow-up even when symptoms have gone

when_to_reach_out: If mental health symptoms started after using a substance or starting a medicine, tell a doctor and say exactly what you've taken. Get urgent help for psychosis, severe agitation, confusion, or thoughts of ending your life.
is_not: The ordinary effects of a substance (being drunk, being high) aren't an induced disorder; it's when the symptoms go beyond that. Symptoms that were present before the substance, or that last long after stopping, point to a primary disorder.
hope_note: When the cause is a substance, stopping it often brings recovery faster than people expect.

sub_sections.title: Which disorders have an induced version
sub_sections.text: Psychotic, bipolar, depressive, anxiety, obsessive-compulsive, sleep, sexual dysfunction, delirium, and neurocognitive disorders. Each is coded under the substance involved.

sub_sections.title: Common culprits
sub_sections.text: Alcohol (depression, anxiety, psychosis, memory problems), stimulants and cannabis (psychosis, anxiety), steroids (mania, depression), sedatives and opioids (depression, delirium in withdrawal), and some prescribed medicines.

content_notes: No dosing, sourcing, or 'how to use' detail. Harm-reduction pointers only to official organizations.
Crisis strip with substance helplines required.
